======================================================================

{{Short description|Undisturbed natural environment}}
{{About|wildland|other uses|The Wilderness (disambiguation){{!}}The Wilderness|and|Wilderness (disambiguation)}}
{{Distinguish|Wildness}}

{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2022}}
{{Environmentalism sidebar}}
[[File:Rockymountainnps (1).jpg|thumb|[[White Goat Wilderness Area]] in [[Canadian Rockies]], Canada.]]
[[File:Little Beaver valley.jpg|thumb|[[Stephen Mather Wilderness]] in the [[United States|U.S.]] state of [[Washington (state)|Washington]].]]
[[File:Innoko Wilderness.jpg|thumb|[[Innoko Wilderness]] in the [[United States|U.S.]] state of [[Alaska]] in the summer.]]
'''Wilderness''' or '''wildlands''' (usually in the [[plurale tantum|plural]]) are [[Earth]]'s [[natural environment]]s that have not been significantly modified by [[human impact on the environment|human activity]], or any [[urbanization|nonurbanized]] [[land]] not under extensive [[agriculture|agricultural]] cultivation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Glossary |publisher=[[National Weather Service]] |url=https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?letter=w |access-date=28 December 2019 |archive-date=15 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315052701/https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?letter=w }}</ref><ref>
{{cite web |url=https://wild.org/main/about/what-is-a-wilderness-area |publisher=[[WILD Foundation]] |title=What is a Wilderness Area |access-date=2009-02-20 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121204162126/http://www.wild.org/main/about/what-is-a-wilderness-area/ |archive-date=4 December 2012}}</ref> The term has traditionally referred to terrestrial environments, though [[human impact on marine life|growing attention]] is being placed on [[marine ecosystem|marine wilderness]]. Recent maps of wilderness<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allan|first1=James R. |last2=Venter|first2=Oscar |last3=Watson|first3=James E. M. |title=Temporally inter-comparable maps of terrestrial wilderness and the Last of the Wild |journal=[[Scientific Data (journal)|Scientific Data]] |date=12 December 2017 |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=170187 |doi=10.1038/sdata.2017.187  |doi-access=free|pmid=29231923 |pmc=5726312 |bibcode=2017NatSD...470187A}}</ref> suggest it covers roughly one-quarter of Earth's terrestrial surface, but is being rapidly degraded by human activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watson |first1=James E.M. |last2=Shanahan |first2=Danielle F. |last3=Di Marco |first3=Moreno |last4=Allan |first4=James |last5=Laurance |first5=William F. |last6=Sanderson |first6=Eric W. |last7=Mackey |first7=Brendan |last8=Venter |first8=Oscar |title=Catastrophic Declines in Wilderness Areas Undermine Global Environment Targets |journal=[[Current Biology]] |date=November 2016 |volume=26 |issue=21 |pages=2929–2934 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2016.08.049 |pmid=27618267 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2016CBio...26.2929W }}</ref> Even less wilderness remains in the [[ocean]], with only 13.2% free from intense human activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Kendall R. |last2=Klein |first2=Carissa J. |last3=Halpern |first3=Benjamin S. |last4=Venter |first4=Oscar |last5=Grantham |first5=Hedley |last6=Kuempel |first6=Caitlin D. |last7=Shumway |first7=Nicole |last8=Friedlander |first8=Alan M. |last9=Possingham |first9=Hugh P. |last10=Watson |first10=James E. M. |title=The Location and Protection Status of Earth's Diminishing Marine Wilderness |journal=[[Current Biology]] |date=August 2018 |volume=28 |issue=15 |pages=2506–2512.e3 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2018.06.010 |pmid=30057308 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2018CBio...28E2506J |hdl=10072/417008 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Some governments establish protection for '''wilderness areas''' by law, not only to [[protected area|preserve what already exists]], but also to promote and advance a natural expression and development. These can be set up in preserves, conservation preserves, national forests, national parks and even in urban areas along rivers, [[gulch]]es or otherwise undeveloped areas. Often these areas are considered important for the survival of certain [[species]], [[biodiversity]], ecological studies, [[nature conservation|conservation]], solitude, and [[recreation]].<ref>{{cite book |title=No Man's Garden |first=Daniel B.|last=Botkin |pages=155–157 |isbn=}}</ref> They may also preserve historic [[genetics|genetic]] traits and provide habitat for wild [[flora (plants)|flora]] and [[fauna (animals)|fauna]] that may be difficult to recreate in [[zoo]]s, [[arboretum]]s, or [[laboratory|laboratories]].

==History==

===Ancient times and Middle Ages===
From a visual arts perspective, nature and wildness have been important subjects in various epochs of world history. An early tradition of [[landscape art]] occurred in the [[Tang Dynasty art|Tang Dynasty]] (618–907). The tradition of representing nature ''as it is'' became one of the aims of [[Chinese painting]] and was a significant influence in Asian art. Artists in the tradition of [[Shan shui]] (lit. ''mountain-water-picture''), learned to depict mountains and rivers "from the perspective of nature as a whole and on the basis of their understanding of the laws of nature{{Nbsp}}… as if seen through the eyes of a bird". In the 13th century, Shih Erh Chi recommended avoiding painting "scenes lacking any places made inaccessible by nature".<ref>[http://www.asia-art.net/chinese_tech_brush.html Chinese brush painting] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060526192019/http://www.asia-art.net/chinese_tech_brush.html |date=26 May 2006 }} Asia-art.net Retrieved on: 20 May 2006.</ref>

For most of [[human history]], the greater part of Earth's terrain was wilderness, and human attention was concentrated on settled areas. The first known laws to protect parts of nature date back to the Babylonian Empire and Chinese Empire. [[Ashoka]], the Great [[Mauryan]] King, defined the first laws in the world to protect [[flora and fauna]] in [[Edicts of Ashoka]] around the 3rd century B.C. In the [[Middle Ages]], the [[Kings of England]] initiated one of the world's first conscious efforts to protect natural areas. They were motivated by a desire to be able to [[Hunting|hunt]] wild animals in private hunting preserves rather than a desire to protect wilderness. Nevertheless, in order to have animals to hunt they would have to protect wildlife from subsistence hunting and the land from villagers gathering firewood.<ref name="History" /> Similar measures were introduced in other European countries.

However, in European cultures, throughout the Middle Ages, wilderness generally was not regarded as worth protecting but rather judged strongly negative as a dangerous place and as a moral counter-world to the realm of culture and godly life.<ref name="Kirchhoff pp.443">{{Cite journal |last=Kirchhoff |first=Thomas |last2=Vicenzotti |first2=Vera |date=August 2014 |title=A Historical and Systematic Survey of European Perceptions of Wilderness |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3197/096327114X13947900181590 |journal=Environmental Values |language=en |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=443–464 |doi=10.3197/096327114X13947900181590 |issn=0963-2719|url-access=subscription }}</ref> "While archaic nature religions oriented themselves towards nature, in medieval Christendom this orientation was replaced by one towards divine law. The divine was no longer to be found in nature; instead, uncultivated nature became a site of the sinister and the demonic. It was considered corrupted by [[Fall of man|the Fall]] (''natura lapsa''), becoming a vale of tears in which humans were doomed to live out their existence. Thus, for example, mountains were interpreted [e.g, by [[Thomas Burnet (theologian)|Thomas Burnet]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Burnet |first=Thomas |url=http://archive.org/details/sacredtheoryofea01burn |title=The Sacred theory of the earth: containing an account of the original of the earth and of all the general changes which it hath already undergone, or is to undergo, till the consumation of all things |date=1719 |publisher=London : Printed for John Hooke |others=Princeton Theological Seminary Library}}</ref>] as ruins of a once flat earth destroyed by the [[Flood]], with the seas as the remains of that Flood."<ref name="Kirchhoff pp.443"/> "If [[paradise]] was early man's greatest good, wilderness, as its antipode, was his greatest evil."<ref>Nash, Roderick Frazier [1967] 2014: Wilderness and the American Mind. Fifth Edition. New Haven & London, Yale University Press / Yale Nota Bene, p. 9</ref>

===15th to 19th century===
Wilderness was viewed by colonists as being evil in its resistance to their control.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Roderick|first=Nash|title=Wilderness and the American mind|date=1973|publisher=Yale University Press|oclc=873974940}}</ref><ref name=":4">Hogan, L. (1994). Department of the Interior. In P. Foster (Ed.), Minding the Body.</ref> The [[puritan]]ical view of wilderness meant that in order for colonists to be able to live in North America, they had to destroy the wilderness in order to make way for their '[[civilized]]' society.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> Wilderness was considered to be the root of the colonists' problems, so to make the problems go away, wilderness needed to be destroyed.<ref name=":3" /> One of the first steps in doing this, is to [[clearcutting|get rid of trees]] in order to clear the land.<ref name=":3" /> Military metaphors describing the wilderness as the "enemy" were used, and settler expansion was phrased as "[conquering] the wilderness".<ref name=":3" />

In relation to the wilderness, [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] were viewed as [[Savage (pejorative term)|savage]]s.<ref name=":5">Dunbar-Ortiz, R. (2014). An Indigenous Peoples' History of the United States. Beacon Press</ref>  The relationship between Native Americans and the land was something colonists did not understand and did not try to understand.<ref>{{cite book| chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctt1pwt77c.12| doi=10.5749/j.ctt1pwt77c.12| chapter=Land as Pedagogy| title=As We Have Always Done| year=2017| pages=145–174| isbn=978-1-4529-5600-8}}</ref> This mutually beneficial relationship was different from how colonists viewed the land only in relation to how it could benefit themselves by waging a constant battle to beat the land and other living organisms into submission.<ref name=":3" /> The belief colonists had of the land being only something to be used was based in Christian ideas.<ref name=":3" /> If the earth and animals and plants were created by a Christian God for human use, then the cultivation by colonists was their God-given goal.<ref name=":5" />

However, the idea that what European colonists saw upon arriving in North America was pristine and devoid of humans is untrue due to the existence of Native Americans.<ref name=":6">Stewart, O. C., Lewis, H. T., & Anderson, K. (2002). Forgotten fires: Native Americans and the transient wilderness. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press.</ref> The land was shaped by Native Americans through practices such as fires.<ref name=":7">Kantor, I. (2007). Ethnic Cleansing and America's Creation of National Parks. Public Land & Resources Law Review, 28, 41-64.</ref> Burning happened frequently and in a controlled manner.<ref name=":6" /> The landscapes seen in the US today are very different from the way things looked before colonists came.<ref name=":6" /> [[wildfire|Fire]] could be used to maintain food, cords, and baskets.<ref name=":6" /> One of the main roles of frequent fires was to prevent the out of control fires which are becoming more and more common.<ref name=":6" />

The idea of wilderness having [[intrinsic value (ethics)|intrinsic value]] emerged in the [[Western culture|Western world]] in the 19th century. [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland|British]] artists [[John Constable]] and [[J. M. W. Turner]] turned their attention to capturing the beauty of the natural world in their paintings. Prior to that, paintings had been primarily of religious scenes or of human beings. [[William Wordsworth]]'s poetry described the wonder of the natural world, which had formerly been viewed as a threatening place. Increasingly the valuing of nature became an aspect of Western culture.<ref name="History">[http://www.spacesfornature.org/greatspaces/conservation.html History of Conservation] BC Spaces for Nature. Retrieved: 20 May 2006.</ref>

By the mid-19th century, in Germany, "Scientific Conservation", as it was called, advocated "the efficient utilization of [[natural resources]] through the application of [[science]] and [[technology]]". Concepts of [[forest management]] based on the German approach were applied in other parts of the world, but with varying degrees of success.<ref name=Wilderness>Akamani, K. (nd). [http://www.abetterearth.org/article.php/1346.html "The Wilderness Idea: A Critical Review."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160830001950/http://www.abetterearth.org/article.php/1346.html |date=30 August 2016 }} A Better Earth.org. Retrieved: 1 June 2006</ref> Over the course of the 19th century, wilderness became viewed not as a place to fear but a place to enjoy and protect; hence came the [[conservation movement]] in the latter half of the 19th century. Rivers were rafted, and mountains were climbed solely for the sake of recreation, not to determine their geographical context.

In 1861, following an intense lobbying by artists of the [[Barbizon school]], the French Waters and Forests Military Agency set an "artistic reserve" in [[Forest of Fontainebleau|Fontainebleau State Forest]]. With a total of 1,097 hectares, it is thought to be the first [[nature reserve]] in the world.{{Citation needed|date=June 2021}}

=== Modern conservation ===
Global conservation became an issue at the time of the dissolution of the [[British Empire]] in [[Africa]] in the late 1940s. The British established great [[Nature reserves|wildlife preserves]] there. As before, this interest in conservation had an economic motive: in this case, [[Big-game hunter|big game hunting]]. Nevertheless, this led to growing recognition in the 1950s and the early 1960s of the need to protect large spaces for wildlife conservation worldwide. The [[World Wildlife Fund]] (WWF), founded in 1961, grew to be one of the largest conservation organizations in the world.<ref name="History" />

Early conservationists advocated the creation of a legal mechanism by which boundaries could be set on human activities in order to preserve natural and unique lands for the enjoyment and use of future generations. This profound shift in wilderness thought reached a pinnacle in the US with the passage of the [[Wilderness Act]] of 1964, which allowed for parts of [[U.S. National Forest]]s to be designated as "wilderness preserves". Similar acts, such as the 1975 [[Eastern Wilderness Areas Act]], followed.

Nevertheless, initiatives for wilderness conservation continue to increase. There is a growing number of projects to [[Tropical rainforest conservation|protect tropical rainforests]] through conservation initiatives. There are also large-scale projects to conserve wilderness regions, such as Canada's [[Boreal Forest Conservation Framework]]. The Framework calls for conservation of 50 percent of the 6,000,000 square kilometres of boreal forest in Canada's north.<ref>Canadian Boreal Initiative [http://www.borealcanada.ca/framework-e.php Boreal Forest Conservation Framework] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071208012102/http://www.borealcanada.ca/framework-e.php |date=8 December 2007 }}. www.borealcanada.ca Retrieved on: 1 December 2007.</ref> In addition to the World Wildlife Fund, organizations such as the [[Wildlife Conservation Society]], the [[WILD Foundation]], [[The Nature Conservancy]], [[Conservation International]], [[The Wilderness Society (United States)]] and many others are active in such conservation efforts.

The 21st century has seen another slight shift in wilderness thought and theory. It is now understood that simply drawing lines around a piece of land and declaring it a wilderness does not necessarily make it a wilderness. All [[landscape]]s are intricately connected, and what happens outside a wilderness certainly affects what happens inside it. For example, [[air pollution]] from [[Los Angeles]] and the California Central Valley affects Kern Canyon and [[Sequoia National Park]]. The national park has miles of "wilderness" but the air is filled with pollution from the valley. This gives rise to the paradox of what a wilderness really is, a key issue in 21st century wilderness thought.

[[File:Ahja jõe ürgorg.jpg|thumb|center|{{center|A view of wilderness in Estonia}}|1144x1144px]]

==National parks==
[[File:El Toro Wilderness.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|[[El Toro Wilderness]] within the [[El Yunque National Forest]] in [[Puerto Rico]].]]
The creation of [[National Park|national park]]s, beginning in the 19th century, preserved some especially attractive and notable areas, but the pursuits of [[commerce]], [[lifestyle (sociology)|lifestyle]], and [[recreation]] combined with increases in [[human population]] have continued to result in human modification of relatively untouched areas. Such human activity often negatively impacts native flora and fauna. As such, to better protect critical habitats and preserve low-impact recreational opportunities, legal concepts of "wilderness" were established in many countries, beginning with the United States (see below).

The first National Park was [[Yellowstone]], which was signed into law by U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant on 1 March 1872.<ref>Mangan, E. [http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/gmdhtml/yehtml/yeabout.html Yellowstone, the First National Park] ''Library of Congress,'' Mapping the National Parks. Retrieved on: 2010-08-12.</ref> The Act of Dedication declared Yellowstone a land "hereby reserved and withdrawn from settlement, occupancy, or sale under the laws of the United States, and dedicated and set apart as a public park or pleasuring ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people".<ref>{{cite web|title=The Magic of Yellowstone|url=http://www.yellowstone-online.com/history/yhfour.html|work=Congressional Acts Pertaining to Yellowstone|access-date=7 December 2011}}</ref>

When national parks were established in an area, the Native Americans that had been living there were forcibly removed so visitors to the park could see nature without humans present.<ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last=Spence |first=Mark David |date=July 1996 |title=Crown of the Continent, Backbone of the World: The American Wilderness Ideal and Blackfeet Exclusion from Glacier National Park |journal=Environmental History |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=29–49 |doi=10.2307/3985155 |jstor=3985155 |bibcode=1996EnvH....1...29S |s2cid=143232340 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/249292740}}</ref> National parks are seen as areas untouched by humans, when in reality, humans existed in these spaces, until settler colonists came in and forced them off their lands in order to create the national parks.<ref name=":8" /> The concept glorifies the idea that before settlers came, the US was an uninhabited landscape.<ref name=":8" /> This erases the reality of Native Americans, and their relationship with the land and the role they had in shaping the landscape.<ref name=":8" /> Such erasure suggests there were areas of the US which were historically unoccupied, once again erasing the existence of Native Americans and their relationship to the land.<ref name=":8" /> In the case of Yellowstone, the Grand Canyon, and Yosemite, the 'preservation' of these lands by the US government was what caused the Native Americans who lived in the areas to be systematically removed.<ref name=":8" />

Historian Mark David Spence has shown that the case of [[Glacier National Park (US)|Glacier National Park]] and the [[Blackfoot Confederacy|Blackfeet]] people who live there is a perfect example of such erasure.<ref name=":8" /> The Blackfeet people had specifically designated rights to the area, but the 1910 Glacier National Park act made void those rights.<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":7" /> The act of 'preserving' the land was specifically linked to the exclusion of the Blackfeet people.<ref name=":8" /> The continued resistance of the Blackfeet people has provided documentation of the importance of the area to many different tribes.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" />

The world's second national park, the [[Royal National Park]], located just 32&nbsp;km to the south of [[Sydney]], [[Australia]], was established in 1879.<ref>New South Wales National Parks & Wildlife Service, ''[http://www.nationalparks.nsw.gov.au/parks.nsf/parkContent/N0030?OpenDocument&ParkKey=N0030&Type=xo "Parks & Reserves: Royal National Park"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060820034120/http://www.nationalparks.nsw.gov.au/parks.nsf/parkContent/N0030?OpenDocument&ParkKey=N0030&Type=Xo |date=20 August 2006 }}''. Accessed 6 December 2011.</ref>

The U.S. concept of national parks soon caught on in [[Canada]], which created [[Banff National Park]] in 1885, at the same time as the transcontinental [[Canadian Pacific Railway]] was being built. The creation of this and other parks showed a growing appreciation of wild nature, but also an economic reality. The railways wanted to entice people to travel west. Parks such as Banff and Yellowstone gained favor as the railroads advertised travel to "the great wild spaces" of North America. When outdoorsman Teddy Roosevelt became president of the United States, he began to enlarge the U.S. National Parks system, and established the National Forest system.<ref name="History" />

By the 1920s, travel across North America by train to experience the "wilderness" (often viewing it only through windows) had become very popular. This led to the commercialization of some of [[National Parks of Canada|Canada's National Parks]] with the building of great hotels such as the [[Banff Springs Hotel]] and [[Chateau Lake Louise]].

Despite their similar name, national parks in [[England and Wales]] are quite different from [[national park]]s in many other countries. Unlike most other countries, in England and Wales, designation as a national park may include substantial settlements and human land uses which are often integral parts of the landscape, and land within a national park remains largely in private ownership. Each park is operated by its own [[national park authority]].

The United States philosophy around wilderness preservation through National Parks has been attempted in other countries.<ref name=":9">Guha, Ramachandra. ""Radical American Environmentalism and Wilderness Preservation: A Third World Critique" (1997)." ''The Future of Nature''. New Haven: Yale UP, 2017. 409-32. Web.</ref> However, people living in those countries have different ideas surrounding wilderness than people in the United States, thus, the US concept of wilderness can be damaging in other areas of the world.<ref name=":9" /> India is more densely populated and has been settled for a long time.<ref name=":9" /> There are complex relationships between agricultural communities and the wilderness.<ref name=":9" /> An example of this is the Project Tiger parks in India.<ref name=":9" /> By claiming areas as no longer used by humans, the land moves from the hands of poor people to rich people.<ref name=":9" /> Having designated tiger reserves is only possible by displacing poor people, who were not involved in the planning of the areas.<ref name=":9" /> This situation places the ideal of wilderness above the already existing relationships between people and the land they live on.<ref name=":9" /> By placing an imperialistic ideal of nature onto a different country, the desire to reestablish wilderness is being put above the lives of those who live by working the land.<ref name=":9" />

==Conservation and preservation in 20th century United States==
By the late 19th century, it had become clear that in many countries wild areas had either disappeared or were in danger of disappearing. This realization gave rise to the [[conservation movement]] in the [[United States]], partly through the efforts of writers and activists such as [[John Burroughs]], [[Aldo Leopold]], and [[John Muir]], and politicians such as [[U.S. President]] [[Theodore Roosevelt|Teddy Roosevelt]].
[[File:Cook Lake Bridger Wilderness.jpg|right|upright=1.25|thumb|Cook Lake in the Bridger Wilderness, [[Bridger-Teton National Forest]], [[Wyoming]], U.S.]]

The idea of protecting nature for nature's sake began to gain more recognition in the 1930s with American writers like [[Aldo Leopold]], calling for a "land ethic" and urging wilderness protection. It had become increasingly clear that wild spaces were disappearing rapidly and that decisive action was needed to save them. Wilderness preservation is central to [[deep ecology]]; a philosophy that believes in an inherent worth of all living beings, regardless of their instrumental utility to human needs.<ref name=barry>{{cite book|title=International Encyclopedia of Environmental Politics|author=John Barry|author2=E. Gene Frankland |publisher=Routledge|date=2002|page=161|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YTB4OMgsxIEC&pg=PA161|isbn=978-0-415-20285-5}}</ref>

Two different groups had emerged within the US environmental movement by the early 20th century: the conservationists and the preservationists. The initial consensus among conservationists was split into "utilitarian conservationists" later to be referred to as conservationists, and "aesthetic conservationists" or preservationists. The main representative for the former was [[Gifford Pinchot]], first Chief of the United States Forest Service, and they focused on the ''proper use of nature,'' whereas the preservationists sought the ''protection of nature from use.''<ref name="Wilderness" /> Put another way, conservation sought to regulate human use while preservation sought to eliminate human impact altogether. The management of US public lands during the years 1960s and 70s reflected these dual visions, with conservationists dominating the Forest Service, and preservationists the Park Service<ref name=Young>{{cite book|last1=Young|first1=Raymond A.|title=Introduction to Forest Science|date=1982|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-471-06438--1|pages=20–21}}</ref>

==Formal wilderness designations==

=== International ===
The [[World Conservation Union]] (IUCN) classifies wilderness at two levels, 1a ([[strict nature reserve]]s) and 1b (Wilderness areas).<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.2305/IUCN.CH.2016.PAG.25.en |title=Wilderness protected areas: Management guidelines for IUCN category 1b protected areas |year=2016 |last1=Locke |first1=H. |last2=Ghosh |first2=S. |last3=Carver |first3=S. |last4=McDonald |first4=T. |last5=Sloan |first5=S.S. |last6=Merculieff |first6=I. |last7=Hendee |first7=J. |last8=Dawson |first8=C. |last9=Moore |first9=S. |last10=Newsome |first10=D. |last11=McCool |first11=S. |last12=Semler |first12=R. |last13=Martin |first13=S. |last14=Dvorak |first14=R. |last15=Armatas |first15=C. |last16=Swain |first16=R. |last17=Barr |first17=B. |last18=Krause |first18=D. |last19=Whittington-Evans |first19=N. |last20=Hamilton |first20=L.S. |last21=Holtrop |first21=J. |last22=Tricker |first22=J. |last23=Landres |first23=P. |last24=Mejicano |first24=E. |last25=Gilbert |first25=T. |last26=MacKey |first26=B. |last27=Aykroyd |first27=T. |last28=Zimmerman |first28=B. |last29=Thomas |first29=J. |isbn=978-2-8317-1817-0}}</ref>

There have been recent calls for the World Heritage Convention to better protect wilderness<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allan |first1=James R. |last2=Kormos |first2=Cyril |last3=Jaeger |first3=Tilman |last4=Venter |first4=Oscar |last5=Bertzky |first5=Bastian |last6=Shi |first6=Yichuan |last7=Mackey |first7=Brendan |last8=van Merm |first8=Remco |last9=Osipova |first9=Elena |last10=Watson |first10=James E.M. |title=Gaps and opportunities for the World Heritage Convention to contribute to global wilderness conservation |journal=Conservation Biology |date=February 2018 |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=116–126 |doi=10.1111/cobi.12976 |pmid=28664996 |bibcode=2018ConBi..32..116A |s2cid=28944427}}</ref> and to include the word wilderness in their selection criteria for Natural Heritage Sites

Forty-eight countries have wilderness areas established via legislative designation as IUCN protected area management Category 1b sites that do not overlap with any other IUCN designation. They are: Australia, Austria, Bahamas, Bangladesh, Bermuda, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Botswana, Canada, Cayman Islands, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cuba, Czech Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Estonia, Finland, French Guiana, Greenland, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Marshall Islands, Mexico, Mongolia, Nepal, New Zealand, Norway, Northern Mariana Islands, Portugal, Seychelles, Serbia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sri Lanka, Sweden, Tanzania, United States of America, and Zimbabwe. At publication, there are 2,992 marine and terrestrial wilderness areas registered with the IUCN as solely Category 1b sites.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://protectedplanet.net/|title=The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA)|date=2016|publisher=IUCN and UNEP-WCMC}}</ref>

Twenty-two other countries have wilderness areas. These wilderness areas are established via administrative designation or wilderness zones within protected areas. Whereas the above listing contains countries with wilderness exclusively designated as Category 1b sites, some of the below-listed countries contain protected areas with multiple management categories including Category 1b. They are: Argentina, Bhutan, Brazil, Chile, Honduras, Germany, Italy, Kenya, Malaysia, Namibia, Nepal, Pakistan, Panama, Peru, Philippines, the Russian Federation, South Africa, Switzerland, Uganda, Ukraine, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, Venezuela, and Zambia.<ref name=":0" />

=== Germany ===
The German National Strategy on Biological Diversity aims to establish wilderness areas on 2% of its terrestrial territory by 2020 (7,140&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>). However, protected wilderness areas in Germany currently only cover 0.6% of the total terrestrial area. In absence of pristine landscapes, Germany counts national parks (IUCN Category II) as wilderness areas.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2019.06.026 |title=A new wilderness for Central Europe? – the potential for large strictly protected forest reserves in Germany |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=237 |pages=373–382 |year=2019 |last1=Brackhane |first1=Sebastian |last2=Schoof |first2=Nicolas |last3=Reif |first3=Albert |last4=Schmitt |first4=Christine B. |bibcode=2019BCons.237..373B |s2cid=199641237 }}</ref> The government counts the whole area of the 16 national parks as wilderness. This means, also the managed parts are included in the "existing" 0,6%. There is no doubt, that Germany will miss its own time-dependent quantitative goals, but there are also some critics, that point a bad designation practice: Findings of disturbance ecology, according to which process-based nature conservation and the 2% target could be further qualified by more targeted area designation, pre-treatment and introduction of [[Megafauna|megaherbivores]], are widely neglected.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schoof|first1=Nicolas|last2=Luick|first2=Rainer|last3=Nickel|first3=Herbert|last4=Reif|first4=Albert|last5=Förschler|first5=Marc|last6=Westrich|first6=Paul|last7=Reisinger|first7=Edgar|year=2018|title=Biodiversität fördern mit Wilden Weiden in der Vision "Wildnisgebiete" der Nationalen Strategie zur biologischen Vielfalt|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326300905|journal=Natur und Landschaft|volume=93|issue=7|pages=314–322}}</ref> Since 2019 the government supports bargains of land that will then be designated as wilderness by 10 Mio. Euro annually.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bmu.de/PM8619|title=Deutschland wird wilder: Neues Förderinstrument Wildnisfonds startet – BMU-Pressemitteilung|website=bmu.de|date=9 July 2019 |language=de|access-date=2019-08-19}}</ref> The German minimum size for wilderness candidate sites is normally 10&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>. In some cases (i.e. swamps) the minimum size is 5&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Opitz|first1=Stefaie|last2=Reppin|first2=Nicole|last3=Schoof|first3=Nicolas|last4=Drobnik|first4=Juliane|last5=Riecken|first5=Uwe|last6=Mengel|first6=Andreas|last7=Reif|first7=Albert|last8=Rosenthal|first8=Gert|last9=Finck|first9=Peter|date=2015|title=Wildnis in Deutschland: Nationale Ziele, Status Quo und Potenziale|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/308117229|journal=Natur und Landschaft|volume=90|pages=406–412}}</ref>

=== Finland ===
{{main|Wilderness areas of Finland}}

[[File:Tsarmitunturin_erämaata_07.JPG|thumb|[[Tsarmitunturi Wilderness Area]]]]
There are twelve wilderness areas in the [[Sami native region (Finland)|Sami native region]] in northern [[Lapland, Finland|Finnish Lapland]]. They are intended both to preserve the wilderness character of the areas and further the traditional livelihood of the Sami people. This means e.g. that reindeer husbandry, hunting and taking wood for use in the household is permitted. As population is very sparse, this is generally no big threat to the nature. Large scale reindeer husbandry has influence on the ecosystem, but no change is introduced by the act on wilderness areas. The World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA) classifies the areas as "VI Protected area with sustainable use of natural resources".{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

=== France ===
Since 1861, the French Waters and Forests Military Agency (Administration des Eaux et Forêts) has strongly protected what was called the « artistic reserve » in Fontainebleau State Forest. With a total of 1,097 hectares, it is known as the first World nature reserve.

Then in the 1950s,<ref>1995 & 1998 National Forests Office internal instructions in application of the last paragraph of article L. 212-2 of the French Forest Act</ref> Integral Biological Reserves (Réserves Biologiques Intégrales, RBI) have been dedicated to a human free ecosystem evolution, in contrast to Managed Biological reserves (Réserves Biologiques Dirigées, RBD), where specific management practiced are applied to conserve vulnerable species or threatened habitats.

Integral Biological Reserves occur in French State Forests or City Forests and are therefore managed by the [[National Forests Office (France)|National Forests Office]]. In such reserves, all harvesting and hunting is forbidden except for exotic species elimination or track safety works to avoid fallen tree risk to visitors (already existing tracks in or on the edge of the reserve).

At the end of 2014,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.onf.fr/onf/sommaire/developpement_durable/actions/20080707-150833-949463/@@index.html|title=L'ONF|date=30 October 2018}}</ref> there were 60 Integral Biological Reserves in French State Forests represented a total area of 111,082 hectares and ten in City Forests for a total of 2,835 hectares.

===Greece===
{{Main|National parks of Greece}}

In Greece there are some parks called "ethniki drimoi" (εθνικοί δρυμοί, national forests) that are under protection of the Greek government. Such parks include [[Mount Olympus|Olympus]], [[Mount Parnassus|Parnassos]] and [[Parnitha]] National Parks.

===New Zealand===
{{Self-contradictory|section|about=the number of areas|date=July 2023}}
There are seven Wilderness Areas in New Zealand as defined by the [[National Parks Act 1980 (New Zealand)|National Parks Act 1980]] and the [[Conservation Act 1987]] that fall well within the IUCN definition. Wilderness areas cannot have any human intervention and can only have indigenous species re-introduced into the area if it is compatible with conservation management strategies.

In [[New Zealand]] wilderness areas are remote blocks of land that have high natural character.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wilderness Areas |url=https://tramper.nz/places/wildernessareas |website=New Zealand Tramper |access-date=28 November 2018}}</ref> The [[Conservation Act 1987]] prevents any access by vehicles and livestock, the construction of tracks and buildings, and all indigenous natural resources are protected.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1987/0065/latest/DLM104684.html#DLM104684|title=Conservation Act 1987 Part 4, Section 20|author=New Zealand Government|date=1987|publisher=New Zealand Government|access-date=2008-10-02}}</ref> They are generally over 400&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> in size.<ref name="lmolloy">{{cite web |last1=Molloy |first1=Les |title=Specially protected areas |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/protected-areas/page-5 |website=[[Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |publisher=[[Ministry for Culture and Heritage]]}}</ref>

Three Wilderness Areas are currently recognised, all on the [[West Coast Region|West Coast]]: Adams Wilderness Area, Hooker/Landsborough Wilderness Area and Paparoa Wilderness Area.<ref name="NZ Gazetteer">{{cite web |title=New Zealand Gazetteer |url= https://gazetteer.linz.govt.nz/ |website=linz.govt.nz |publisher=[[Land Information New Zealand]]}}</ref>

===United States===
{{Main|National Wilderness Preservation System|List of wilderness areas in the United States}}

[[File:Image-Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge New Jersey03.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.15|The Great Swamp of New Jersey, donated for federal protection by concerned residents, was designated as the first wilderness refuge in the United States in 1960.]]

In the United States, a Wilderness Area is an area of federal land set aside by an [[United States Congress|act of Congress]]. It is typically at least 5,000 acres (about 8&nbsp;mi<sup>2</sup> or 20&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>) in size.<ref name="Pulaski">{{Cite web |last=Savannah |first=Mailing Address: 41 Cockspur Island Road |last2=Us |first2=GA 31410 Phone:219-4233 Contact |title=Wilderness - Fort Pulaski National Monument (U.S. National Park Service) |url=https://www.nps.gov/fopu/learn/nature/wilderness.htm |access-date=2026-08-14 |website=www.nps.gov |language=en}}</ref> Human activities in wilderness areas are restricted to scientific study and non-mechanized recreation; horses are permitted but mechanized vehicles and equipment, such as cars and bicycles, are not.

The United States was one of the first countries to officially designate land as "wilderness" through the [[Wilderness Act]] of 1964. The Wilderness Act is an important part of wilderness designation because it created the legal definition of wilderness and established the National Wilderness Preservation System. The Wilderness Act defines wilderness as "an area where the earth and its community of life are untrammelled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain".<ref>{{cite web|title=Wilderness Act of 1964|url=http://wilderness.net/index.cfm?fuse=NWPS&sec=legisact|work=Wilderness.net|access-date=7 December 2011|archive-date=11 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211070549/http://www.wilderness.net/index.cfm?fuse=NWPS&sec=legisact}}</ref>

Wilderness designation helps preserve the natural state of the land and protects flora and fauna by prohibiting development and providing for non-mechanized recreation only.

The first administratively protected wilderness area in the United States was the Gila National Forest. In 1922, [[Aldo Leopold]], then a ranking member of the U.S. Forest Service, proposed a new management strategy for the Gila National Forest. His proposal was adopted in 1924, and 750,000 acres of the Gila National Forest became the [[Gila Wilderness]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Aldo Leopold|url=http://www.wilderness.net/index.cfm?fuse=feature0105|work=Prominent Figures in Wilderness History|access-date=7 December 2011|archive-date=29 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111229234947/http://www.wilderness.net/index.cfm?fuse=feature0105}}</ref>

[[Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge|The Great Swamp in New Jersey]] was the first formally designated wilderness refuge in the United States. It was declared a wildlife refuge on 3 November 1960. In 1966 it was declared a [[National Natural Landmark]] and, in 1968, it was given wilderness status. Properties in the swamp had been acquired by a small group of residents of the area, who donated the assembled properties to the federal government as a park for perpetual protection. Today the refuge amounts to {{convert|7600|acre|km2}} that are within thirty miles of [[Manhattan]].<ref>U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. [http://www.fws.gov/northeast/greatswamp/ Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge]. Retrieved on: 7 June 2008.</ref>

[[File:Latir Peak Wilderness.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.15|[[Latir Peak Wilderness]], in [[New Mexico]]]]
While wilderness designations were originally granted by an Act of Congress for Federal land that retained a "primeval character", meaning that it had not suffered from human habitation or development, the [[Eastern Wilderness Act]] of 1975 extended the protection of the NWPS to areas in the eastern states that were not initially considered for inclusion in the Wilderness Act. This act allowed lands that did not meet the constraints of size, roadlessness, or human impact to be designated as wilderness areas under the belief that they could be returned to a "primeval" state through preservation.<ref>"[http://www.ncmountaintreasures.org/info/wilderness_act.html The Wilderness Act of 1964] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100923101919/http://ncmountaintreasures.org/info/wilderness_act.html |date=23 September 2010 }}". Western North Carolina's Mountain Treasures. Retrieved on 16 June 2010.</ref>

Approximately {{convert|107500000|acre|km2}} are designated as wilderness in the United States. This accounts for 4.82% of the country's total land area; however, 54% of that amount is found in Alaska (recreation and development in Alaskan wilderness is often less restrictive), while only 2.58% of the lower continental United States is designated as wilderness. As of 2023 there are [[List of wilderness areas of the United States|806 designated wilderness areas]] in the United States ranging in size from Florida's [[Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge|Pelican Island]] at {{convert|5|acre|m2}} to Alaska's Wrangell-Saint Elias at {{convert|9078675|acre|km2}}.

Several U.S. States have Wilderness Preservation systems that resemble the National Wilderness Preservation System. Notable among these are [[Protected areas of California|California State Wilderness system]], New York (Primarily in the [[Adirondack Park]]), and [[Maryland Wildland|Maryland Wildland Preservation System]].

===Western Australia===
In Western Australia,<ref>[[Department of Conservation and Land Management]] Policy Statement No 62, Identification and management of Wilderness and surrounding areas.</ref> a wilderness area is an area that has a wilderness quality rating of 12 or greater and meets a minimum size threshold of 80&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> in temperate areas or 200&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> in arid and tropical areas. A wilderness area is gazetted under section 62(1)(a) of the Conservation and Land Management Act 1984 by the Minister on any land that is vested in the Conservation Commission of Western Australia.

==International movement==
{{see also|Rewilding}}

[[File:Monument Valley 2.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.15|[[Monument Valley]] in [[Utah]], United States]]
At the forefront of the international wilderness movement has been The [[WILD Foundation]], its founder [[Ian Player]] and its network of sister and partner organizations around the globe. The pioneer World Wilderness Congress in 1977 introduced the wilderness concept as an issue of international importance, and began the process of defining the term in biological and social contexts. Today, this work is continued by many international groups who still look to the World Wilderness Congress as the international venue for wilderness and to The WILD Foundation network for wilderness tools and action. The WILD Foundation also publishes the standard references for wilderness professionals and others involved in the issues: ''Wilderness Management: Stewardship and Protection of Resources and Values'', the ''International Journal of Wilderness'', ''A Handbook on International Wilderness Law and Policy'' and ''Protecting Wild Nature on Native Lands'' are the backbone of information and management tools for international wilderness issues.

The Wilderness Specialist Group within the [[World Commission on Protected Areas]] (WTF/WCPA) of the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] (IUCN) plays a critical role in defining legal and management guidelines for wilderness at the international level and is also a clearing-house for information on wilderness issues.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.iucn.org/theme/protected-areas/wcpa/what-we-do/wilderness|title=Wilderness|date=2016-02-08|work=IUCN|access-date=2017-03-22}}</ref> The IUCN Protected Areas Classification System defines wilderness as "A large area of unmodified or slightly modified land, and/or sea retaining its natural character and influence, without permanent or significant habitation, which is protected and managed so as to preserve its natural condition ([[strict nature reserve|Category 1b]])". The WILD Foundation founded the WTF/WCPA in 2002 and remains co-chair.

==Extent==
[[File:Togiak Wilderness.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.15|The [[Ahklun Mountains]] and the [[Togiak Wilderness]] within the [[Togiak National Wildlife Refuge]] in the [[United States|U.S.]] state of [[Alaska]].]]

The most recent efforts to map wilderness<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Allan|first1=James R.|last2=Venter|first2=Oscar|last3=Watson|first3=James E. M.|date=2017-12-12|title=Temporally inter-comparable maps of terrestrial wilderness and the Last of the Wild|journal=Scientific Data|language=en|volume=4|issue=1|page=170187|doi=10.1038/sdata.2017.187|doi-access=free|pmid=29231923|issn=2052-4463|pmc=5726312|bibcode=2017NatSD...470187A}}</ref> show that less than one quarter (~23%) of the world's wilderness area now remains, and that there have been catastrophic declines in wilderness<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Watson|first1=James E. M.|last2=Shanahan|first2=Danielle F.|last3=Di Marco|first3=Moreno|last4=Allan|first4=James|last5=Laurance|first5=William F.|last6=Sanderson|first6=Eric W.|last7=Mackey|first7=Brendan|last8=Venter|first8=Oscar|date=2016-11-07|title=Catastrophic Declines in Wilderness Areas Undermine Global Environment Targets|journal=Current Biology|language=English|volume=26|issue=21|pages=2929–2934|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2016.08.049|issn=0960-9822|pmid=27618267|doi-access=free|bibcode=2016CBio...26.2929W }}</ref> extent over the last two decades. Over 3 million square kilometers (10 percent) of wilderness was converted to human land-uses. The Amazon and Congo rain forests suffered the most loss. Human pressure is extending into almost every corner of the planet.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Venter|first1=Oscar|last2=Sanderson|first2=Eric W.|last3=Magrach|first3=Ainhoa|last4=Allan|first4=James R.|last5=Beher|first5=Jutta|last6=Jones|first6=Kendall R.|last7=Possingham|first7=Hugh P.|last8=Laurance|first8=William F.|last9=Wood|first9=Peter|last10=Fekete|first10=Balázs M.|last11=Levy|first11=Marc A.|date=2016-08-23|title=Sixteen years of change in the global terrestrial human footprint and implications for biodiversity conservation|journal=Nature Communications|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|article-number=12558|doi=10.1038/ncomms12558|doi-access=free|pmid=27552116|issn=2041-1723|pmc=4996975|bibcode=2016NatCo...712558V}}</ref> The loss of wilderness could have serious implications for biodiversity conservation.

According to a previous study, ''Wilderness: Earth's Last Wild Places,'' carried out by [[Conservation International]], 46% of the world's land mass is wilderness. For purposes of this report, "wilderness" was defined as an area that "has 70% or more of its original vegetation intact, covers at least {{convert|10000|km2|sqmi|sp=us}} and must have fewer than five people per square kilometer".<ref>Conservation International (2002) [https://www.conservation.org/NewsRoom/pressreleases/Pages/120402-Two-Year-Study-Identifies-Earths-Most-Pristine-Regions.aspx Global Analysis Finds Nearly Half The Earth Is Still Wilderness]. Retrieved on 6 Nov 2017.</ref> However, an [[IUCN]]/[[UNEP]] report published in 2003, found that only 10.9% of the world's land mass is currently a Category 1 [[Protected Area]], that is, either a ''[[strict nature reserve]]'' (5.5%) or ''protected wilderness'' (5.4%).<ref>Chape, S., S. Blyth, L. Fish, P. Fox and M. Spalding (compilers) (2003). ''2003 United Nations List of Protected Areas.'' [[IUCN]], Gland, Switzerland and Cambridge, UK and [[World Conservation Monitoring Centre|UNEP-WCMC]], Cambridge, UK. [http://www.unep.org/PDF/Un-list-protected-areas.pdf PDF] {{Webarchive|url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20040701214854/http://www.unep.org/PDF/Un-list-protected-areas.pdf |date=1 July 2004 }}</ref> Such areas remain relatively untouched by humans. Of course, there are large tracts of lands in national parks and other protected areas that would also qualify as wilderness. However, many protected areas have some degree of human modification or activity, so a definitive estimate of true wilderness is difficult.

The [[Wildlife Conservation Society]] generated a ''human footprint'' using a number of indicators, the absence of which indicate wildness: human population density, human access via roads and rivers, human infrastructure for agriculture and settlements and the presence of industrial power (lights visible from space). The society estimates that 26% of the Earth's land mass falls into the category of "Last of the wild". The wildest regions of the world include the [[Arctic]] [[Tundra]], the [[Siberia]] [[Taiga]], the [[Amazon rainforest]], the [[Tibetan Plateau]], the Australia [[Outback]] and deserts such as the [[Sahara]], and the [[Gobi]].<ref>Wildlife Conservation Society. 2005. ''State of the Wild 2006: A Global Portrait of Wildlife, Wildlands and Oceans.'' Washington, D.C. Island Press. pp. 16 &17.</ref> However, from the 1970s, numerous [[geoglyph]]s have been discovered on deforested land in the Amazon rainforest, leading to claims about [[Pre-Columbian era|Pre-Columbian]] civilizations.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/01/15/world/americas/land-carvings-attest-to-amazons-lost-world.html?_r=1|title=Once Hidden by Forest, Carvings in Land Attest to Amazon's Lost World|author=Simon Romero|newspaper=The New York Times|date=14 January 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |journal=Antiquity |date=2009 |volume=83 |issue=322 |pages=1084–1095 |title=Pre-Columbian geometric earthworks in the upper Purús: a complex society in western Amazonia |author=Martti Pärssinen |author2=Denise Schaan |author3=Alceu Ranzi |name-list-style=amp |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00099373 |s2cid=55741813 }}</ref> The BBC's ''[[Unnatural Histories (TV series)|Unnatural Histories]]'' claimed that the Amazon rainforest, rather than being a pristine wilderness, has been shaped by man for at least 11,000 years through practices such as [[forest gardening]] and [[terra preta]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b0122njp|title=Unnatural Histories – Amazon|publisher=BBC Four}}</ref>

The percentage of land area designated wilderness does not necessarily reflect a measure of its [[biodiversity]]. Of the last natural wilderness areas, the taiga—which is mostly wilderness—represents 11% of the total land mass in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref>University of Manitoba Taiga Biological Station. 2004. [http://www.wilds.mb.ca/taiga/tbsfaq.html Frequently answered questions.] Retrieved: 2006-07-04.</ref> [[Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|Tropical rainforest]] represent a further 7% of the world's land base.<ref>Rainforest Foundation US. 2006. [http://www.rainforestfoundation.org/kids.php Commonly asked questions.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061001143602/http://www.rainforestfoundation.org/kids.php |date=1 October 2006 }} Retrieved: 2006-07-04.</ref> Estimates of the Earth's remaining wilderness underscore the rate at which these lands are being developed, with dramatic declines in biodiversity as a consequence.
{{Clear}}

==Critique==
[[File:Cedar Mtn Wilderness.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.15|[[Cedar Mountain Wilderness]] in northern [[Utah]], United States.]]

The American concept of wilderness has been criticized by some nature writers. For example, [[William Cronon]] writes that what he calls a wilderness ethic or cult may "teach us to be dismissive or even contemptuous of such humble places and experiences", and that "wilderness tends to privilege some parts of nature at the expense of others", using as an example "the mighty canyon more inspiring than the humble marsh".<ref name=Cronon>[http://history.wisc.edu/cronon/Trouble_with_Wilderness_Main.html The Trouble with Wilderness] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927053842/http://history.wisc.edu/cronon/Trouble_with_Wilderness_Main.html |date=27 September 2011 }} University of Wisconsin-Madison. Retrieved: 28 January 2007.</ref> This is most clearly visible with the fact that nearly all U.S. National Parks preserve spectacular canyons and mountains, and it was not until the 1940s that a swamp became a national park—[[the Everglades]]. In the mid-20th century national parks started to protect [[biodiversity]], not simply attractive scenery.

Cronon also believes the passion to save wilderness "poses a serious threat to responsible [[environmentalism]]" and writes that it allows people to "give ourselves permission to evade responsibility for the lives we actually lead{{Nbsp}}... to the extent that we live in an urban-industrial civilization but at the same time pretend to ourselves that our real home is in the wilderness".<ref name = "Cronon" />

[[Michael Pollan]] has argued that the wilderness ethic leads people to dismiss areas whose wildness is less than absolute. In his book ''Second Nature'', Pollan writes that "once a landscape is no longer 'virgin' it is typically written off as fallen, lost to nature, irredeemable."<ref>Pollan, Michael (2003). ''Second Nature: A Gardener's Education'' p. 188. Grove Press. {{ISBN|978-0-8021-4011-1}}.</ref> Another challenge to the conventional notion of wilderness comes from Robert Winkler in his book, ''Going Wild: Adventures with Birds in the Suburban Wilderness''. "On walks in the unpeopled parts of the suburbs", Winkler writes, "I've witnessed the same wild creatures, struggles for survival, and natural beauty that we associate with true wilderness."<ref>Winkler, Robert. (2003). ''Going Wild: Adventures with Birds in the Suburban Wilderness'' National Geographic {{ISBN|978-0-7922-6168-1}}.</ref> Attempts have been made, as in the [[Pennsylvania Scenic Rivers]] Act, to distinguish "wild" from various levels of human influence: in the Act, "wild rivers" are "not impounded", "usually not accessible except by trail", and their watersheds and shorelines are "essentially primitive".<ref>Pennsylvania Scenic Rivers Act (P.L. 1277, Act No. 283 as amended by Act 110, May 7, 1982)</ref>
 
Another source of criticism is that the criteria for wilderness designation is vague and open to interpretation. For example, the Wilderness Act states that wilderness must be roadless. The definition given for roadless is "the absences of roads which have been improved and maintained by mechanical means to insure relatively regular and continuous use".<ref>{{cite book |last=Durrant |first=Jeffrey O. |title=Struggle over Utah's San Rafael Swell: Wilderness, National Conservation Areas, and National Monuments |date=2007 |publisher=University of Arizona Press |isbn=978-0-8165-2669-7 |page=43}}</ref> However, there have been added sub-definitions that have, in essence, made this standard unclear and open to interpretation, and some are drawn to narrowly exclude existing roads.

Coming from a different direction, some criticism from the [[Deep Ecology]] movement argues against conflating "wilderness" with "wilderness reservations", viewing the latter term as an oxymoron that, by allowing the law as a human construct to define nature, unavoidably voids the very freedom and independence of human control that defines wilderness.<ref>{{cite book|title=Deep Ecology for the 21st Century |date=1995 |publisher=Shambhala |location=Boston |isbn=978-1-57062-049-2 |pages=345, 339–355 |author=Thomas Birch |author-link=The Incarceration of Wildness: Wilderness Areas as Prisons|editor=George Sessions}}</ref> True wilderness requires the ability of life to undergo [[speciation]] with as little interference from humanity as possible.<ref>{{cite book |title=Deep Ecology for the 21st Century |date=1995 |publisher=Shambhala |location=Boston |isbn=978-1-57062-049-2 |pages=323, 323–330 |author=George Sessions |author-link=Introduction: Wilderness, the Wild, and Conservation Biology}}</ref> [[Anthropologist]] and scholar on wilderness Layla Abdel-Rahim argues that it is necessary to understand the principles that govern the economies of mutual aid and diversification in wilderness from a non-anthropocentric perspective.<ref>{{cite book |title=Children's Literature, Domestication, and Social Foundation: Narratives of Civilization and Wilderness |date=2015|publisher=Routledge|location=New York |isbn=978-0-415-66110-2 |author=Layla AbdelRahim|author-link=Layla AbdelRahim}}</ref>

Others have criticized the American concept of wilderness as rooted in [[white supremacy]], ignoring Native American perspectives on the natural environment and excluding people of color from narratives about human interactions with the environment. Many early conservationists, such as [[Madison Grant]], were also heavily involved in the [[eugenics movement]]. Grant, who worked alongside President [[Theodore Roosevelt]] to create the [[Bronx Zoo]], also wrote ''[[The Passing of the Great Race]]'', a book on eugenics that was later praised by Adolf Hitler. Grant is also known to have featured [[Ota Benga]], a [[Mbuti]] man from Central Africa, in the Bronx Zoo monkey house exhibit.<ref>{{cite book |title=Defending the Master Race: Conservation, Eugenics, and the Legacy of Madison Grant |date=2009 |publisher=University Press of New England |location=Burlington |isbn=978-1-584-65715-6 |author=Jonathan Spiro |author-link=Johnathan Spiro}}</ref> [[John Muir]], another important figure in the early conservation movement, referred to African-Americans as "making a great deal of noise and doing little work", and compared Native Americans to unclean animals who did not belong in the wilderness.<ref>{{cite web |title= Shades of Darkness: Race and Environmental History |date=11 April 2005 |url=https://historycooperative.org/journal/shades-of-darkness-race-and-environmental-history/ |access-date= 7 February 2021}}</ref> Environmental history professor Miles A. Powell of Nanyang Technological University has argued that much of the early conservation movement was deeply tied to and inspired by a desire to preserve the [[Nordic race]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Vanishing America: Species Extinction, Racial Peril, and the Origins of Conservation |date=2016 |publisher=Harvard University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-674-97156-1 |author=Miles A. Powell |author-link=Miles A. Powell}}</ref> Prakash Kashwan, a political science professor at the University of Connecticut who specializes in environmental policies and [[environmental justice]], argues that the racist ideas of many early conservationists created a narrative of wilderness that has led to "fortress conservation" policies that have driven Native Americans off of their land. Kashwan has proposed conservation practices that would allow Indigenous people to continue using the land as a more just and more effective alternative to fortress conservation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kashwan |first1=Prakash |editor-first1=Jennifer |editor-last1=Weeks |title=American environmentalism's racist roots have shaped global thinking about conservation |date=2 September 2020 |doi=10.64628/AAI.fvyvpvvgv |url=https://theconversation.com/american-environmentalisms-racist-roots-have-shaped-global-thinking-about-conservation-143783 |access-date= 7 February 2021}}</ref> The idea that the natural world is primarily made up of remote wilderness areas has also been criticized as classist, with environmental sociologist [[Dorceta Taylor]] arguing that this leads to experiencing wilderness becoming a privilege, as working-class people are often unable to afford transportation to wilderness areas. She further argues that, due to poverty and lack of access to transportation caused by [[systemic racism]], this perception is also rooted in racism.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Rise of the American Conservation Movement: Power, Privilege, and Environmental Protection |date=2016 |publisher=Duke University Press |location=Durham |isbn=978-0-8223-7397-1 |author=Dorceta E. Taylor}}</ref>

=== Human–nature dichotomy ===
Another critique of wilderness is that it perpetuates the human-nature dichotomy. The idea that nature and humans are separate entities can be traced back to European colonial views. To European settlers, land was an inherited right and was to be used to profit.<ref>{{Cite book |first1=Walter C. |last1=Opello |first2=Stephen J. |last2=Rosow |title=The nation-state and global order: a historical introduction to contemporary politics|date=2004|publisher=Lynne Rienner|isbn=1-58826-289-8|oclc=760384471}}</ref> While native groups saw their relationship with the land in a more holistic view, they were eventually subjected to European property systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Park|first=K-Sue|date=2016|title=Money, Mortgages, and the Conquest of America|journal=Law & Social Inquiry|volume=41|issue=4|pages=1006–1035|doi=10.1111/lsi.12222|s2cid=157705999|issn=0897-6546}}</ref> Colonists from Europe saw the American landscape as wild, savage, dark, [etc.] and thus needed to be tamed in order for it to be safe and habitable. Once cleared and settled, these areas were depicted as "Eden itself".<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=William.|first=Cronon|title=Uncommon ground: rethinking the human place in nature|date=1996|publisher=W.W. Norton & Co|isbn=0-393-31511-8|oclc=36306399}}</ref> Yet the native peoples of those lands saw "wilderness" as that when the connection between humans and nature is broken.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Anderson|first=M. Kat|title=Tending the Wild|date=2005-06-14|publisher=University of California Press|doi=10.1525/9780520933101|isbn=978-0-520-93310-1}}</ref> For native communities, human intervention was a part of their ecological practices.

There is a historical belief that wilderness must not only be tamed to be protected but that humans also need to be outside of it.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Claus|first=C. Anne|title=Drawing the Sea Near|date=2020-11-03|publisher=University of Minnesota Press|doi=10.5749/j.ctv1bkc3t6|isbn=978-1-4529-5946-7|s2cid=230646912}}</ref> In order to clear certain areas for conservation, such as national parks, involved the removal of native communities from their land.<ref name=":1" /> Some authors have come to describe this type of conservation as conservation-far, where humans and nature are kept separate. The other end of the conservation spectrum then, would be conservation-near, which would mimic native ecological practices of humans integrated into the care of nature.<ref name=":2" />

Most scientists and conservationists agree that no place on earth is completely untouched by humanity, either due to past occupation by [[indigenous people]], or through global processes such as [[climate change]] or [[pollution]]. Activities on the margins of specific wilderness areas, such as [[Wildfire|fire]] suppression and the interruption of [[Bird migration|animal migration]], also affect the interior of wildernesses.
